thread.title: Facebook: Do Share Buybacks Mean Growth Is Dead? - Facebook (NASDAQ:FB)

author: Shock Exchange
title: Facebook: Do Share Buybacks Mean Growth Is Dead? - Facebook (NASDAQ:FB)
text:
Source: Fortune
I am bearish on the market and falling technology stocks could help my modest short positions in non-tech names. If hedge funds take a beating on Facebook ( FB ), Apple ( AAPL ), and Netflix ( NFLX ), they may sell other stocks to preserve capital. Selling in tech names could beget selling in the overall market, so my theory goes.
FB is down over 20% Y/Y. Amid the carnage, the company announced it was increasing the amount authorized under its share repurchase program by $9 billion:
Facebook [NASDAQ: FB] discloses a $9B increase in the amount authorized under its share repurchase program; shares +0.7% after-hours. The $9B adds to the $15B the company previously had authorized under the buyback program since it commenced in 2017.
JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) CEO Jamie Dimon intimated buybacks are good when a stock is cheap. Stock buybacks have come under scrutiny, especially for companies that employed debt to fund them. I would not consider FB cheap. The stock trades at around 6.6x run-rate revenue (Q2 and Q3 2018 revenue annualized). The company has $41 billion of cash on hand and generated free cash flow ("FCF") of $12 billion through the first nine months of the year. With no debt, Facebook can more than afford an additional $9 billion in buybacks.
Is Facebook Still A Growth Stock? The question I have is, "What is CEO Mark Zuckerberg signaling to investors?" I believe Zuckerberg is signaling FB may no longer be a growth stock. Growth companies invest in R&D and capital expenditures to help grow the business. When a company would rather buy its own shares instead of expand its existing operations, then it could portend fewer growth opportunities. Facebook could counter that it is difficult to efficiently put $41 billion in capital to work.
Over 2 billion people use Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram and Messenger monthly. The ability for advertisers to reach that many people in one fell swoop is difficult to ignore. I would hasten to say that Facebook's competition is limited pursuant to its market reach. However, its monthly active users ("MAUs") appear to have plateaued. Q3 2018 MAUs of 2.3 billion were up 10% Y/Y, but only grew 2% sequentially.
The average revenue per user ("ARPU") was up 20%. This explains why revenue grew 33% Y/Y, outstripping MAU growth. ARPU grew by low single digits Q/Q, and could ring in slow growth in revenue and ARPU going forward. That said, macroeconomic headwinds abound. RV shipments fell 11% in the month of October and are down 1% through the first nine months of the year. They are expected to be down about 5% for full year 2018.
A decline in RV shipments preceded the last two recessions. These big ticket discretionary items could be one of the first things consumers chop if the economy falters. Corporate advertising could be the next discretionary item to go. That would not be good for digital advertising platforms like Facebook, Twitter ( TWTR ) or Snapchat ( SNAP ). A flat yield curve portends another recession could be on the horizon, and it could be amplified by the debt binge corporations have embarked on over the past decade:
Total outstanding non-financial corporate debt has increased by over $2.5 trillion or 40% since its 2008 high; it now represents over 45% of GDP.
Highly-indebted names like General Electric ( GE ), Teva ( TEVA ) and Bausch Health ( BHC ) have cut costs to the bone to help service their debt. Others will likely tighten the belt to help repay debt used for acquisitions and share repurchases at market heights. The fallout will likely be lower ad spending.
Facebook's saving grace is it continues to empower small businesses and entrepreneurs. I believe entrepreneurs and small businesses will continue to advertise with Facebook because the platform represents an efficient use of capital. They can potentially get the word out about a product or an event without having a sizeable marketing staff or public relations budget. The push/pull between a decline in corporate ads and a potential rise in small business ads could define the narrative going forward.
Price Discovery Investors have crowded into FB over the years. The growth in the economy, the transition from traditional advertising to digital advertising, and the melt up in financial markets have proven FB bulls right. Now that the Fed is removing the punch bowl and recessionary pressures abound, traditional valuation metrics could come into play. Is nearly 7x revenue a fair price for a company whose revenue growth will likely stagnate going forward?
Secondly, there is little evidence of how Facebook's revenue stream will hold up in a recession. Zuckerberg is good at managing growth, but can he manage a business with declining revenue and falling margins? What happens if Facebook has to fight with Twitter or traditional media outlets for a declining pool of ad revenue? How much value are investors willing to put on a stock that has lost its momentum? Is the proper valuation metric a multiple of revenue, EBITDA or earnings? Whatever the math is, I believe it will result in a price far less than $137. It could be due to a lower multiple, declining revenue and earnings, or less flows into financial markets.
Conclusion In April, I suggested investors sell FB due to regulatory scrutiny over its business model. It is down by double digits since then. Regulators continue to scrutinize Facebook amid allegations that (1) its executives gave certain developers special access to data and (2) considered charging developers for the privilege. However, a pending decline in discretionary spending could be the more immediate risk to the stock. Sell FB.
Disclosure: I am/we are short GE, TEVA, BHC.
